summary.primary_diagnosis: Acute decompensated heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
summary.hospital_course: A 79-year-old female with known heart failure with reduced ejection fraction was admitted with three days of increasing dyspnea, orthopnea, and a 4 kg weight gain. Physical examination demonstrated elevated jugular venous pressure, bibasilar crackles, and bilateral pitting edema to the mid-shin, with markedly elevated NT-proBNP. She was diuresed with intravenous furosemide, achieving a net negative fluid balance of 4.2 liters over five days, leading to symptom resolution and a discharge weight of 71.4 kg (her documented dry weight). Medication reconciliation identified ibuprofen as a contributor to decompensation and declining renal function; it was discontinued and replaced with acetaminophen. Metformin dose was reduced in the context of CKD stage 3a with an eGFR of 44 mL/min/1.73 m2. Low-dose sacubitril-valsartan was initiated on day four and tolerated well, with systolic blood pressure remaining above 105 mmHg. Serum creatinine stabilized at 1.4 mg/dL over the final 48 hours. Physiotherapy assessed her as requiring a rolling walker for safe ambulation; she became short of breath after walking approximately 15 meters on the day prior to discharge. A outpatient basic metabolic panel is required within 7 days.
summary.condition_at_discharge: Euvolemic at documented dry weight (71.4 kg), hemodynamically stable with systolic blood pressure remaining above 105 mmHg, serum creatinine stable at 1.4 mg/dL. Shortness of breath resolved at rest; requires a rolling walker for safe ambulation.

interactions.description: Loop diuretics can reduce renal clearance of metformin and raise its plasma concentration.
interactions.recommendation: Check renal function after any diuretic dose increase.

interactions.description: Additive hypotension, particularly during uptitration of either agent.
interactions.recommendation: Uptitrate one agent at a time and monitor blood pressure and symptoms.

interactions.description: Renin-angiotensin system blockade can reduce renal function, raising metformin accumulation and lactic-acidosis risk in chronic kidney disease.
interactions.recommendation: Monitor renal function; reduce the metformin dose if eGFR falls below 45.

education.plain_language_summary: You were in the hospital because your heart was not pumping blood as well as it should, causing extra water to build up in your body. We adjusted your medicines to help your heart pump better and remove extra fluid. You will need to weigh yourself every morning, take your medicines as directed, and go to your scheduled doctor visits. A home health nurse will visit you at home, and ride support is arranged for your appointments.
medication_instructions: Furosemide (water pill): Take 40 mg once daily in the morning. Dose increased from 20 mg once daily to help remove extra fluid.
Metoprolol succinate: Take 25 mg once daily. Continued to help your heart beat steadily.
Apixaban (blood thinner): Take 5 mg twice daily (morning and evening). Continued to prevent blood clots.
Metformin: Take 500 mg twice daily with meals. Dose reduced from 1000 mg twice daily to protect your kidneys.
Sacubitril-valsartan: Take 24/26 mg twice daily (morning and evening). NEW heart medicine to help your heart pump better.
Acetaminophen: Take 650 mg as needed for mild pain. NEW safe pain reliever.
STOP TAKING Ibuprofen: Do NOT take ibuprofen. It causes your body to hold water and can harm your kidneys and heart.
activity_and_diet: Weigh yourself every morning right after waking up and using the bathroom, before eating or drinking. Write your weight on a log.
Eat a low-salt diet. Do not add table salt to your meals, and avoid high-salt canned or packaged foods.
Raise your legs on pillows when sitting down to help reduce leg swelling.
Take short walks if you feel up to it, but rest whenever you feel tired or short of breath.
red_flag_symptoms: Call 911 right away if you have severe chest pain, pass out, or cannot catch your breath at rest.
Call your doctor if you gain more than 3 pounds in 1 day or 5 pounds in 1 week.
Call your doctor if your ankles, legs, or belly swell more than usual.
Call your doctor if you feel short of breath while lying flat or wake up gasping for air.
Call your doctor if you feel dizzy or lightheaded when standing up.
caregiver_instructions: Since you live alone, home health nursing will visit you to check your vitals, leg swelling, and draw blood for lab tests.
Expect a phone call check-in from your care team within 2 to 3 days (48 to 72 hours).
Expect a call from a pharmacist within 7 days to review your medications.
Keep your daily weight log and medicine list next to your telephone so you have them ready for your calls.
